title: April deliberations lay out the conditions for cuts, a near hold or consecutive hikes
summary: Governing Council agreed to keep the overnight rate at 2.25% on 29 April. The 13 May summary explains how members could endorse the same setting while seeing quite different possible paths. With existing US tariffs unchanged and oil prices easing along the futures curve, a rate close to the current level could support adjustment and bring inflation back to 2%. More trade restrictions could weaken demand enough to justify cuts. Persistently high oil prices, spreading into broader costs and expectations, could instead require successive increases. These were conditional alternatives around a baseline, not a timetable or an announcement of equally probable outcomes (Considerations for monetary policy and Policy decision).

After the fourth-quarter contraction caused largely by inventory drawdown, early first-quarter indicators had been weak, but later data suggested growth had resumed close to January’s projection. Consumption and government spending accounted for much of domestic demand. Business investment made a small contribution and exports remained constrained by sectoral tariffs and policy uncertainty. The quarterly Business Outlook Survey showed stronger sales and investment expectations and sentiment returning to levels seen before the US tariffs. Managers nevertheless reported limited capacity to raise selling prices in a soft economy. Improved expectations about orders and weak pricing power could therefore coexist. The survey had recently proved a useful leading indicator, though members did not assume that investment intentions would convert fully into expenditure (Canadian economy and inflation outlook).

The housing and labour evidence reinforced that distinction. Low resale activity reflected cyclical uncertainty as well as slower population growth, weaker investor demand and persistent affordability or suitability problems. A lower policy rate could influence financing without promptly resolving a mismatch between households and the homes available. Job finding was weak, and unemployment had ranged between 6.5% and 7% for several months. Population ageing reduced participation while slower population growth limited growth of the labour force. An unchanged unemployment rate in that setting could conceal weak hiring. Members judged these conditions would restrict wage pressure and the ability of businesses to restore margins by raising consumer prices (Canadian economy and inflation outlook).

CPI inflation rose to 2.4% in March as petrol prices jumped. The trimmed and median measures continued to indicate easing underlying pressure. The proportion of components rising faster than 3% declined, and the share rising more slowly than 1% increased. Rent and food remained conspicuous exceptions. Some energy-intensive services such as air travel showed effects, but there was little broad transmission at that point. Short-term expectations had risen alongside petrol and grocery costs while longer-run beliefs remained anchored. Households faced a real affordability loss even if underlying inflation stayed close to target. Monetary policy could influence the persistence of that loss through subsequent pricing behaviour, but it could not produce more oil (Canadian economy and inflation outlook and Considerations for monetary policy).

Global oil was above US$100 per barrel when the April outlook was prepared. Given a subsequent easing of oil prices and no further tariff change, Council projected CPI around 3% in April and a return to 2% in early 2027. Real GDP was expected to grow 1.2% in 2026, 1.6% in 2027 and 1.7% in 2028. Rising exports and investment would contribute to growth slightly above potential and gradually absorb slack. Canada’s energy export revenue partly offset costs to consumers and businesses, leaving aggregate GDP growth broadly similar to the January outlook even though its composition shifted. Equity markets had rebounded, yields were above pre-war levels but changed modestly relative to January, and the Canadian dollar remained near US$0.73 (International economy and Canadian economy and inflation outlook).

Council stressed two conditions for looking through the direct shock. First, inflation had been close to target for more than a year and a half and there was spare capacity. Second, the baseline energy shock would fade. If available capacity had been overestimated, the output gap might close sooner and firms could pass on more costs. If the conflict persisted, bottlenecks and higher inputs would work through supply chains over a longer period. Recent experience of high inflation might make households more responsive to prominent price increases. Council regarded 2.25% as at the stimulative end of the neutral-rate range and judged there was room for patience initially. This was a judgement about the starting point and the horizon of policy, sensitive to both assumptions (Considerations for monetary policy).

The adverse oil scenario explored the interaction of prices, output and the currency. Persistent energy costs could spread past the direct petrol contribution. The amount of tightening warranted would depend partly on the investment response in Canada’s energy sector and how the exchange rate adjusted. A simultaneous adverse trade shock could slow sales and impede pass-through, so one cannot add a fixed number of increases for oil and subtract a fixed number for tariffs. Members differed on the likelihood of trade and energy outcomes and therefore on the most probable future path. Their agreement was to preserve room to respond, with relatively small adjustments under the central case and potentially larger moves if one of the adverse paths became more likely (Considerations for monetary policy and Policy decision).

questions.question: Was the apparent disinflation beyond energy widespread enough to restrain later cost pass-through?
questions.detail: Reconstruct CPI component shares, trimmed inflation and median inflation using the releases available at the decision. Track whether components with weak initial demand subsequently showed lower pass-through from freight and fuel costs than more buoyant sectors. Keep food, rent, air travel and direct petrol contributions visible, since headline affordability and broad price-setting can give different signals.

questions.question: Did firms convert better investment expectations into actual capacity outside energy production?
questions.detail: Compare original business survey intentions with orders, imports of capital goods and realised investment in tariff-exposed industries, energy producers and domestically oriented firms. Control for policy announcements during the interval. Increased energy investment could support aggregate demand without indicating that exporters exposed to US tariffs had regained confidence or productive capacity.

questions.question: Which risk did investors price when the conditional range of policy paths became public?
questions.detail: Examine meeting-dated rates and options around the April decision and May publication, alongside crude prices, the Canadian dollar and US trade news. Separate a shift in the most likely rate from greater pricing of both tails. A nearly unchanged median path could coexist with substantially more expensive protection against either rate cuts following tariffs or hikes after prolonged energy disruption.
